article.text:
THE price of electricity traded on the Wholesale Electricity Spot Market (WESM) climbed in October, as power outages tightened supply margins, according to the Independent Electricity Market Operator of the Philippines (IEMOP).
At a briefing on Wednesday, Rica O. Cagnayo, a trading operations for market simulation and analysis staffer at IEMOP, said the average spot price system-wide rose 18.4% month on month to P8.79 per kilowatt-hour (kWh).
Available supply increased 1.4% to 20,493 megawatts (MW) while demand rose 4.3% to 14,793 MW.
Luzon recorded the steepest price increase of 51.2% to P7.83 per kWh. Available supply declined 0.9% to 14,972 MW while demand increased 6.9% to 10,580 MW.
“Tighter supply margins due to rising demand and reduced generation availability, coupled with planned and forced outages, led to higher prices,” Ms. Cagnayo said.
Meanwhile, electricity prices in the Visayas declined 9.9% month on month to P11.19 per kWh, as supply rose 8.7% to 2,392 MW while demand slipped 0.6% to 2,087 MW.
She attributed the decline in prices to improved supply availability and reduced demand.
In Mindanao, WESM prices fell 12.3% to P11.06 per kWh. Supply rose 8.1% to 3,129 MW while demand decreased 2.9% to 2,126 MW.
“Similar conditions were observed in Mindanao where higher supply and reduced demand contributed to slightly lower market prices despite alerts and forced outages,” Ms. Cagnayo said.
IEMOP manages the WESM, where power firms can buy electricity when their long-term supply contracts fall short of meeting customer demand.
Isidro E. Cacho, Jr., IEMOP’s vice-president for trading operations, said electricity prices have risen significantly this year.
Prices in the Visayas and Mindanao hit around P11 per kWh in October, up from the P3 to P6 per kWh range a year earlier. Meanwhile, prices on Luzon were at P7 to P8 per kWh over the same period.
“So, what drove the prices? Of course, it was a combination of factors, including the increase in demand, coupled with the supply constraints we have seen, which translated into higher market prices,” he said. — Sheldeen Joy Talavera

MANILA, Philippines — Users of liquefied petroleum gas may get an early Christmas gift this month as large cuts in international prices could lead to a rollback in local LPG prices.
Contract prices in global markets, as determined by Saudi oil giant Aramco, have plummeted by $90 per metric ton after the Democratic Party routed the Republican Party of US President Donald Trump in last week’s midterm elections, Regasco president Arnel Ty said yesterday.
If the price trend continues until the end of the month, LPG prices may fall in December by anywhere between P5 and P6 per kilo.
But Ty raised the possibility of implementing the rollback as early as this month, depending on what transpires in Thursday’s meeting between LPG players and the Department of Energy.
“Probably, because of this softening of prices, we might experience an advanced rollback for LPG,” Ty told “Money Talks” on One News.
“But we have to communicate first with the DOE that if any brand will have an advanced rollback, it should be credited as a rollback of December’s contract price,” he added.
Household cooking has become more expensive ever since the Middle East war broke out in late February.
Demand for LPG is down by as much as 30 percent this year, according to Ty, though he is confident that vendors could recover their losses.
“We believe we can recoup that once the international market price of LPG starts going down,” he said.
Motorists are enjoying lower crude prices, with the price of gasoline plunging this week by as much as P17 per liter and diesel by P4 per liter.

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine economy is expected to grow by just 2.6 to three percent this year, well below government expectations, as stubborn inflation, weak consumer spending and delayed infrastructure projects threaten to prolong the slowdown into 2027.
Nomura lowered its 2026 gross domestic product (GDP) growth forecast to three percent from 3.8 percent, while BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, trimmed its projection to 2.6 percent from three percent.
Both estimates fall below the government’s 3.5 to 4.5 percent growth target.
BMI also cut its 2027 forecast to four percent from 4.5 percent, citing expectations of a slow recovery.
GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced in the country. It grew by just 2.1 percent in the third quarter, slower than the revised 2.4 percent in the preceding quarter and the weakest reading since early 2021.
Growth averaged 2.5 percent in the first nine months.
“We expect the weak momentum to carry over into 2027,” BMI said, warning that elevated inflation, higher borrowing costs and subdued consumer confidence would continue to weigh on demand.
Inflation accelerated to 7.8 percent in October, reducing households’ purchasing power. Consumer spending growth slowed to 2.4 percent in the third quarter from 2.9 percent previously.
BMI also warned that adverse weather and El Niño could further disrupt agriculture after farm output contracted by 4.8 percent in the third quarter, potentially undermining rural incomes and consumption.
The research firm expects a stronger recovery only in 2027, when government infrastructure spending could gain momentum. However, ongoing investigations into questionable flood-control projects could prolong delays.
Nomura was more optimistic about the near-term outlook, forecasting fourth-quarter growth above four percent as public spending accelerates and the economy benefits from a low comparison base a year earlier.
It noted that fixed investment contracted by a smaller 4.4 percent in the third quarter, compared with 13.7 percent in the second, suggesting that construction and equipment spending were beginning to stabilize.
Still, Nomura said the combined effects of energy-price pressures and infrastructure-related governance concerns had made the Philippines “the region’s big underperformer this year.”
BMI expects technology exports, supported by demand linked to artificial intelligence, to provide some relief through 2027.
However, both firms see the pace of infrastructure spending and the direction of inflation as crucial to the recovery.

Don’t panic.” On national debt, which has reached an alarming 66 percent of GDP, he called the absolute amount “just a number in the air. It doesn’t mean anything.” These are the words uttered by an entitled heir who has never had to struggle with rising prices nor felt the consequences of a weakening economy.
BBM wants us to believe that all is fine as he nonchalantly dismisses public anxiety. Why should we trust him? Four years into his presidency and Marcos has demonstrated neither the competence nor political will needed to keep the economy growing at pace.
